title: How to Choose a GCSE Maths Tutor: What Parents Should Look For
description: A practical parent checklist for choosing a GCSE Maths tutor: diagnosis, exam-board knowledge, lesson structure, feedback, online teaching and how to compare.

children: Choosing a GCSE Maths tutor is easier when you start with the problem you want tuition to solve. A student who has missed key algebra needs something different from a student who understands the content but loses marks through method selection, careless working or exam timing. The best first question is therefore not ‘Who is the most impressive tutor?’ but ‘How will this tutor identify what is actually going wrong?’
Start with the Problem the Tutor Needs to Solve

Before regular lessons begin, a tutor should gather evidence. Recent school work, mock papers, topic tests or a short diagnostic task can show whether the priority is missing knowledge, fluency, reasoning, exam technique or accuracy.
Knowledge gaps:
missing or insecure mathematical content that needs explicit teaching.
Fluency gaps:
a method is understood but too slow or error-prone to use reliably.
Reasoning gaps:
the student knows techniques individually but struggles to choose or combine them in unfamiliar problems.
Exam-performance gaps:
marks are lost through interpretation, working, checking or time management rather than missing content.

For example, two students can both lose marks on quadratics for very different reasons. One may not understand factorising; another may factorise correctly but fail to recognise when the method is appropriate. Good tuition should respond differently to those two students.

Six Questions to Ask a GCSE Maths Tutor

Subject knowledge matters, but parents should also ask how that knowledge will be turned into a repeatable teaching process. Useful questions are specific enough that the answer reveals how the tutor actually works.
Which exam boards and tiers do you teach?
Ask whether the tutor works regularly with the specification and paper style your child actually uses.

How will you diagnose weaknesses?
Look for something more precise than asking the student which topics they dislike.

What does a typical lesson involve?
The answer should include active student practice, not only explanation or worksheet supervision.

How do you use marked work?
Useful feedback should shape subsequent teaching rather than disappear after a score is given.
Useful feedback should shape subsequent teaching rather than disappear after a score is given.
What happens between lessons?
Ask whether homework, marking, questions or resources are included and what the student is expected to complete independently.

How will I know whether tuition is working?
Progress should be described through evidence such as improved accuracy, independence, topic performance or timed-paper work, not vague reassurance.

You are looking for a coherent process rather than a perfect sales answer: diagnose the problem, teach it clearly, make the student practise, check whether it transfers to new questions and use the result to plan what happens next.
How to Compare Tutoring Costs Fairly

Tutoring prices vary considerably, so a single market-rate figure quickly becomes misleading. Compare the actual service rather than the headline hourly number and ask for the current price directly from the tutor or provider.
Lesson format and length:
compare like with like: one-to-one, small group, session duration and frequency can materially change the service.
What the fee includes:
ask whether planning, homework, marking, parent feedback or support between lessons is included or charged separately.
Policies and commitments:
check cancellation terms, block-booking requirements, notice periods and any group-size arrangements before comparing total cost.

A higher or lower fee is not evidence of quality on its own. The useful comparison is what happens around the lesson, how well the teaching matches the student and whether progress is being checked rather than assumed.

What Good GCSE Maths Tuition Should Look Like

Within the first few lessons, the student should be doing substantial mathematics rather than listening for most of the session. Explanations should lead into guided examples, independent attempts and feedback that targets the reasoning as well as the final answer.
A clear objective:
the tutor and student should know what the lesson is trying to improve.
Explicit modelling:
difficult methods should be demonstrated with the reasoning made visible.
Guided practice:
the student attempts similar work with prompts reduced as understanding improves.
Independent questions:
the tutor checks whether the method can be selected and applied without step-by-step prompting.
Error analysis:
mistakes are classified and corrected rather than simply marked wrong.
A next step:
the lesson ends with a clear decision about what needs retrieval, practice or teaching next.

The balance will change over time. Early sessions may contain more diagnosis and explicit teaching; later sessions can use mixed questions and timed papers to test whether the student can select methods independently.
Choosing an Online GCSE Maths Tutor

Online tuition does not become effective simply because it uses a digital whiteboard. The important question is whether the technology makes the student’s thinking visible enough for the tutor to diagnose and respond to it.
Work visibility:
the tutor needs to see calculations and written working, not only hear final answers.
Low-friction sharing:
handwritten work, screenshots or uploaded files should be easy to review when needed.
Reliable communication:
audio, video and screen sharing should work consistently enough not to consume the teaching time.
Purposeful digital tools:
whiteboards or graphing tools should clarify mathematics rather than add novelty for its own sake.
A workable routine:
lesson times and submission of work should fit the student’s school commitments well enough to be sustainable.

A student should still be writing, calculating, explaining and correcting work. Screen sharing and whiteboards are useful when they support that process, not when they turn the lesson into a presentation.
Look for Growing Independence, Not Dependence

The long-term goal is for the student to make better decisions without the tutor beside them. A strong tutor gradually removes prompts and checks whether methods, reasoning and checking routines transfer to unfamiliar questions.
Correct previous errors before starting new work
Keep a short log of recurring mistakes and methods
Practise mixed questions so the topic is not given away
Explain working aloud when a method feels uncertain
Use full papers periodically to test timing, stamina and method selection
These habits make tuition more valuable because they continue between lessons and remain useful after the GCSE course itself.

A good GCSE Maths tutor should be able to explain what the student is struggling with, why the chosen lesson is addressing it and what evidence will show whether it has improved. Compare tutors on that process, their relevant experience and the clarity of what is included in the service, rather than unsupported promises or a headline price alone.
